lines: Avery Brooks
+1 (555) 010-3319 | avery.brooks@example.com | example.com/in/abrooks
Date of birth: 9 Jan 1998 | Nationality: Brazilian
EDUCATION
Eastmoor University | B.S. in Statistics | Metro City, USA | Sep 2016 - May 2020
EXPERIENCE
Pinecrest Insurance | Junior Analyst | Metro City, USA | Jul 2020 - Jul 2022
- Owned the claims backlog report and the weekly numbers the claims managers used.
- Analyzed 18 months of call-center data; my findings moved two agents to the evening peak and cut average hold time from 9 to 5 minutes.
- Wrote the team's SQL style guide and review checklist, which cut query errors found in review by half.

- Automated the monthly fraud-flag extract while also maintaining the team calendar, answering ad hoc questions from sales, updating onboarding documents and covering the help desk on Fridays, which saved the fraud team 10 hours a month.
Brightcart Retail | Data Analyst | Metro City, USA | Aug 2022 - Jun 2025
- Improved reporting efficiency by 90% by moving the monthly revenue report to scheduled SQL queries.
- Found customers with no orders by left-joining the orders table to the customers table and counting rows with a null customer name.
- Wrote data-quality checks on the 40 most-used tables, catching 15 broken loads before they reached a dashboard.
- Presented the quarterly customer review to the leadership team, and two of its three recommendations were funded in the next budget.
- Reported the national conversion rate as the simple average of 14 regional conversion rates, without weighting by regional traffic.
- Built the weekly retention dashboard for 2.4M customers that marketing used to retarget lapsed buyers, lifting 90-day repeat purchase from 22% to 27%.
PROJECTS
City Bike-Share Demand Study | Independent Project | Python, SQL | Jan 2025 - Present
- Modeled hourly bike-share demand for 120 stations from 2 years of public trip data, forecasting next-day demand within 12% mean absolute error.
- Compared the forecast with the operator's rebalancing schedule: empty-station hours fell from 310 to 205 a week in a replay of last summer.
- Published the notebooks and a short write-up, which the city's open-data team linked from its bike-share page.
Food Pantry Visit Analysis | Volunteer, Team of 3 | Excel, SQL | Mar 2023 - Aug 2023
- Mapped 14 months of pantry visits by hour and day, so the pantry moved one volunteer shift and cut the Saturday line from 50 to 20 minutes.
- Cleaned 9,000 handwritten visit logs into a single table and matched repeat visitors, giving the pantry its first count of unique households.
- Built a retention dashboard for about 2.4 million shoppers that raised repeat purchases by nearly a quarter.
SKILLS
Tools: SQL, Python, Excel
Methods: dashboards, forecasting, metric design, data-quality checks

items.says: Check that the email and profile URL are real, working professional contact details.
items.because: The example-domain email and short profile URL look like placeholders and can make the resume appear unfinished.

items.says: Remove the date of birth and nationality unless an application requires them.
items.because: They take up space and disclose personal information not generally needed to assess qualifications.

items.says: Clarify the scope and impact of the claims backlog report and weekly numbers.
items.because: “Owned” and “used” are broad and do not convey scale or outcome.

items.says: Support the implied connection between the call-center findings, staffing change and hold-time reduction.
items.because: The before-and-after measurement, observation period and other possible changes are not explained.

items.says: Define a query error and explain how the reduction by half was measured.
items.because: Without a baseline, comparison period or review volume, the percentage is hard to evaluate.

items.says: Reduce the list of calendar, sales, onboarding and help-desk duties.
items.because: It dilutes the more relevant automation work.

items.says: Explain how the 10 hours per month was estimated and whether the automation accounts for the saving.
Define the efficiency measure and comparison behind the 90% improvement.
items.because: Without a before-and-after measure, the figure is difficult to interpret or verify.

items.says: Counting null customer names is an unreliable way to find customers with no orders.
items.because: A missing customer name could cause records to be misclassified; the method should use a reliably populated identifier.

items.says: Account for duplicate records in the no-orders analysis.
items.because: Duplicates raise questions about the correctness of the result.

items.says: Give the time period and clarify what it means to have “caught” a broken load.
items.because: Detection and prevention of a bad dashboard are different outcomes.

items.says: Substantiate the figures of 40 tables and 15 broken loads.
Clarify your contribution to the quarterly presentation.
items.because: The current wording leaves your role unclear.

items.says: Distinguish recommendations being funded from causing the funding decision.
items.because: The connection between the recommendations and the decision is unclear.

items.says: The simple average of regional conversion rates can misstate the national rate.
items.because: It gives regions equal weight regardless of their traffic.

items.says: Define the dashboard population, measurement period, 90-day window and calculation of the 22% and 27% rates.
Do not imply that dashboard use by itself caused the repeat-purchase increase.
items.because: A dashboard used for retargeting does not establish a lift without evidence such as a control or comparison group.

items.says: Clarify which results of the ongoing project are complete and when they were produced.
items.because: The project is listed as ongoing.

items.says: Define the denominator or normalization for “within 12% mean absolute error.”
items.because: MAE is usually expressed in the units being forecast, so a percentage needs an explanation.

items.says: Explain the time-based train/test split and forecast baseline.
Make clear that the drop in empty-station hours was from a simulation or backtest, not a real-world reduction.
items.because: The result came from a replay.

items.says: Define “empty-station hours” and explain the replay assumptions.
items.because: Comparing a forecast with a schedule alone does not prove a schedule change would produce the reported outcome.

items.says: Add a working project link so reviewers can verify the work.
Describe the city’s link accurately without implying endorsement or adoption unless it occurred.
Explain how wait times were measured and how the shift change relates to the shorter line.
items.because: The bullet attributes an operational result to the analysis without showing how the connection was established.

items.says: State your own contribution to cleaning and matching records.
items.because: The project was done by a three-person team.

items.says: Explain how ambiguous records and repeat-visitor matches were handled.
Ensure the work with pantry visitors’ records was authorized and privacy-conscious.
items.because: The records concern pantry visitors.

items.says: The retention-dashboard result duplicates the Brightcart result almost exactly.
items.because: It looks like a copy-paste error in an unrelated project.

items.says: A dashboard for 2.4 million shoppers is implausible in the food-pantry project context.
items.because: The stated shopper-scale result does not appear to belong to this project.

items.says: Make the listed tools more specific and verifiable.
items.because: “SQL, Python, Excel” does not show which tools or techniques you can actually use.

items.says: Make the broad methods more specific and verifiable.
items.because: They do not show which techniques you can actually use.

items.says: Check that “metric design” is consistent with the work shown.
items.because: The national conversion-rate calculation undermines that claim until it is resolved.
